cells.tense: You are here with your own sense of what's fair, and it is working.
cells.act: act on the private sense of what is right
cells.ask: Settle the small case that keeps reopening — no announcement, no rehearsal — the way you'd settle it if nobody were watching.
cells.core:
There's a pull in you toward something you honestly want, and the gathering is going well: thoughts that were scattered are lining up into something you could move on. Underneath sits a sense of what's fair that you don't have to reason your way to. You walk into an uneven room and it's plain, and what to do about it is plain too.

That inner compass is what to spend this week. Trust it once, somewhere small — the decision you keep reopening, the moment you notice someone got less than they were owed. Let what you feel make the call and act before the day ends. Decide one case the way you'd decide it unwatched, and you'll learn whether the compass led you right.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel what's fair before you can argue it.
cells.verb: gathering scattered thoughts into one line you can move on
cells.place: the pull toward the light you're honestly drawn to

cells.tense: You keep counting on a version of the light that keeps moving just farther off.
cells.act: do the next piece at the speed you can keep for a month, not the speed you can keep for a day
cells.ask: Pick the next real step and take it at a monthly pace, not the sprint you picture at your best — slow enough that you could still hold it later.
cells.core:
The pull toward what you want is real, and the gathering has gone past gathering. Thoughts get re-collected and restacked: the plan rechecked, the argument rehearsed, the decision reopened at midnight. The light you steer by keeps drifting farther out, and you keep measuring the distance instead of setting the pace.

What's missing is rhythm, not resolve. Pick the next real piece of this and do it slowly — a speed you could still hold next month, not the burst you imagine at your best — then keep that pace whatever the week throws. Your careful head gets less air; the part of you that simply cares gets a turn. Go at a walk, so the direction comes from what you actually value, not from how fast you could be done.

cells.tense: You felt the pull toward something brighter, and you set it down a while back.
cells.act: spend an hour with the thing you love without a task attached to it
cells.ask: Give something you love a real hour, then walk away with nothing to show — no task, no note, nothing collected.
cells.core:
There was a light you were moving toward, and the chase stopped. Your thinking about it is still arranged around that old pursuit — order kept for a door you no longer stand at. You'd have to check twice to name what you want now.

So don't reach for the big want. Give a loved thing a real hour this week — a table, a walk, an album — and stop when it ends. Not a step toward anything, not something you'll report later. What arrives isn't direction; it's the texture of an hour that needed no use, warmth that shows up without being chased. That's enough for now. The large want can wait another week.

cells.tense: You are steering by a light you've stopped counting as yours.
cells.act: let the gladness go out to the room
cells.ask: Say the glad thing out loud where the others can hear it — one plain sentence, handed over, nothing more.
cells.core:
The pull toward what's bright does its work in you quietly — you know which way to lean and you lean. The gathering runs too, and if someone asked you'd say that's just how your head works, not something you're doing. In a meeting you'll take two scattered points and close them into one clean line, the group moves on, and nobody — including you — marks whose line it was.

The hand on the tiller is yours. Let it show once: name the good thing you notice nearby, said aloud so the others catch it too. A sentence will do. It's small, and it's the difference between carrying something in private and passing it on — the first stays with you, the second keeps moving after you've gone.

attempts.check: The seat's balanced face ('Recognized, not given; remembered, not arrived') is the one the record hedges — it borrows a religious lineage the signature itself never names, so I did not use it. A reader could fairly say the gathering-I'm-blaming in the Too Much cell might be mostly real external pressure, so I kept the accusation on the recounting, not on their life. Every ask is a small self-contained act that still teaches something if the read is wrong: pausing before a decision narrows nothing, the month-pace piece is just slower, the photo has no stake, and the three-word why has no audience. The sentence serving me more than them was an earlier 'your compass was always private' ending — cut; it flattered the reader's picture of themselves instead of handing them anything.
